newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Algeria's economy shows glimmers of light.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Algeria's economy shows glimmers of light.

text.p: In the violence-scarred Algerian capital, foreign embassies are slowly reopening, or increasing their staff.
Visits by foreign businessmen, still made under tight security, are more frequent and no longer simply focus on the oil and gas sector.

There are signs that after five years of violence which scared away investors and changed Algeria's approach to economic problems, the North African country is finally, if cautiously, moving toward a free market.
Internal conflict on the speed of liberalisation is still evident, but President Liamine Zeroual has given clear signals.
Privatisation must be speeded up, more investment sought, industry made more efficient or allowed to die, and food self-sufficiency improved dramatically.

"The most significant and difficult crisis that our country must triumph over is an economic one," he told 500 officials, bankers, union leaders and others at a conference that wound up early this month.

While some Algerian politicians opposed the meeting as a rubber stamp for Zeroual's ideas, several Algiers-based Western analysts said it brought out with unprecedented openness the facts on Algeria's economy.
"And it allowed people with differing opinions to hear the problems and give their views," said one.
ALGERIA'S PROBLEMS ARE MANIFOLD
The problems are clear.

Nearly 30 years of socialist management ran up $32 billion in foreign debt to take Algeria near to bankruptcy. Without debt rescheduling its debt servicing in 1994 would have totalled more than $9 billion while its energy income, which is 97 percent of foreign earnings, would have earned only around $8.4 billion.
With the benefit of rescheduling of around $12 billion of debts the debt service ratio dropped to 34 percent of foreign earnings in 1994 but rose again to 40 percent in 1995.
Its food import bill is around $2.5 billion a year for its population of 29 million, with the same amount again for medicines, raw materials and spares for ageing and absolete machinery.

The food bill includes 2.4 million tonnes of hard wheat -- half the world's external trade in that grain -- together with 4.9 million tonnes of other cereals and derivatives, 270,000 tonnes of milk and milk products, and 800,000 tonnes of sugar and its byproducts.
Subsidies on most essentials have been removed and the authorities admit life is harder for most, despite inflation being brought to about 19 percent this year from 30 percent in July 1995.
Sabotage in the conflict between Moslem fundamentalists and security forces has inflicted more than $2 billion in damage on the economy according to the Interior Ministry.
Most of the 400 state enterprises outside the energy sector are inefficient, operating often at only 35 percent capacity, government officials say.

The treasury pumped 500 billion dinars ($9 billion) into them over seven years. Yet industrial output in the first six months of this year fell seven percent, earning just $366 million in exports, against the same period in 1995.
Within these "holdings" more than 33,000 medium and small firms employ 1.2 million people, 30 percent of the workforce.
WORLD BANK URGES MASS PRIVATISATION

World Bank experts have urged mass privatisation of an estimated 1,350 saleable firms. But Abderrahmane Mebtoul, head of the Privatisation Council, said this week that sales would be on a case by case basis.
"It is a matter of carrying out a privatisation...with the aim of avoiding social upheaval jeopardising all the reform process." Fears of adding to unrest haunt the authorities.

"The government is always going to be deeply sensitive to social pressures and social unrest. You might get away with laying people off at a small hotel but you would have problems doing it with a big firm," said one economic analyst.
Algeria has so far sold off 10 companies, including a small hotel. But now the authorities say some money-losing small businesses run by local authorities will be closed down.
"That is a new step, and could show they mean business," the analyst said.
OIL WINDFALL WILL HELP

Besides at least a perception of improved security, Algeria has an oil windfall to keep its security forces well equipped and paid, and maintain a minimal social security net for the 2.1 million who are already unemployed.
Its oil output is estimated at 830,000 barrels a day and its budget is based on an oil price of $15 to $17 a barrel. Current prices are $24 a barrel.

Next month, its Maghreb pipeline to Spain and Portugal should come on stream, pumping gas at nearly 20 km per hour towards thirsty markets. It hopes its 30 billion cubic metres of annual gas exports will reach 60 billion by the year 2,000.
"By then, our annual energy income will be $16 billion," one Algerian official told Reuters in the same week as a German minister paid a second visit to look at investment.

With thousands of hectares of land idle after a so-called "agrarian revolution", a presidential paper suggests that cultivating potatoes on 50,000 hectares for off-season exports to Europe and Canada could earn enough to pay the cereal import bill.
Algeria's authorities have detailed their problems and scope for investment in blunt terms. They say they need another 1.2 million dwellings now, and 800,000 more by the year 2,000.

That means building 300,000 each year, at a cost of 250 to 300 billion dinars ($4.6 to $5.5 billion). Now, as one Western economist commented, the authorities have to balance the demands of financial bodies like the World Bank and IMF in building up their reserves, estimated at $2 billion, and using foreign currency to stimulate building and provide jobs.

In one ray of hope, for the first time since independence from France in 1962, the annual population growth rate has fallen under two percent. Pessimists say one reason for the drop is that young people, in a Moslem land, are unable to find houses and jobs to enable them to marry.
